sources.news_title: Missouri to get up to $150M in landmark Meta social media settlement
sources.text:
In a landmark settlement, Meta Platforms Inc. — the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp — agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion in penalties over claims it endangered children with addictive social media platforms to 47 states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories.
Missouri will receive up to $150 million as part of the Meta settlement, according to a Missouri Attorney General Aug. 26 press release.
The Attorney General’s Office called the settlement “one of the largest protection settlements in history outside the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s.”
The settlement may be a turning point in the social media industry, where the biggest players have mostly eluded regulatory scrutiny despite allegations that social media products are as addictive and harmful to children and teenagers as cigarettes, digital casinos and pornography.
The settlement, filed Aug. 26, essentially ends a federal trial in California, where four states were seeking roughly $200 billion over similar accusations of harm to children. Meta will initially pay about $12 billion, but that increases to $17.1 billion if Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube also settle and agree to financial penalties and product changes. Meta still faces numerous lawsuits in jurisdictions across the U.S.
On top of the financial penalties for violating federal child privacy and states’ consumer protection laws, Meta agreed to make major changes to its products as part of the settlement. The lengthy, 120-page settlement can be found here.
Those changes include safety features the company is required to implement on Facebook and Instagram to protect children, like hard daily time limits and “Productive Pauses.” There will also be “Nighttime Blocks” restricting children’s access from midnight to 6 a.m. and limited school-time access. Meta has also promised robust age verification measures and safer, age-appropriate content controls, as well as stronger user-friendly parental controls.
Meta also agreed to install limits on social comparison features like beauty filters and “like” counts, which have been linked to poor mental health outcomes in children and teenagers, according to the press release.
In an Aug. 26 statement, Meta Platforms laid out that it had reached an agreement with 52 attorneys general and planned to build on “longstanding efforts to empower parents and support teens.”
“Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta,” the company said in the statement.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway said the social media issues extend far beyond one company, and Meta’s settlement marked the first major platform to reach a resolution on youth safety.
As part of the settlement, Missouri will receive $100 million to $150 million, according to the AG press release.
“Meta’s willingness to acknowledge the harm and take meaningful corrective action is an important step forward for the safety of children across the country,” Hanaway said in the release. “By implementing enforceable time limits, nighttime protections, age verification tools, and healthier content controls, Meta is setting a new benchmark for the industry.”
In the company statement on the settlement, Meta urged TikTok and YouTube to put the same safety measures in place. The company said its protections will only be effective if other social media companies join rank in limiting teenagers’ social media activities.
“While this is an important step, the fact is that teens move fluidly between dozens of apps a day,” Meta representatives said in the statement. “All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place, because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another.
“For meaningful progress to happen, we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard.”
According to the press release, attorneys general across the country began cooperating in 2021 to investigate the social media industry. After a bipartisan, nationwide investigation “found that Meta designed Instagram’s features to addict children while internally documenting the resulting mental health harms and failing to warn parents,” the states sued Meta individually and as part of a federal lawsuit. This settlement resolves those cases and claims.
Included in the settlement are attorneys general of: Alabama, Alaska, American Samoa, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Northern Mariana Islands, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

sources.news_title: Instagram and Facebook to be made safer for children in the US...but not the UK
sources.text:
Children in the UK will not be given the additional protection measures Meta has pledged to roll out in the US after reaching an eye-watering settlement in America.
An $18bn (£13.24bn) deal has been agreed with Facebook and Instagram owner Meta following claims brought by 29 US states that argued the platforms harmed children. It comes after the company denied all allegations throughout the proceedings.
On top of the financial settlement, Meta has guaranteed that it will introduce significant protections for children and teen accounts on its apps.
How Birmingham could become Britain’s first 20mph city
Implementing a 20mph speed limit on Birmingham’s non-A-class roads would be a “life-saving measure”, a West Midlands transport boss has said.
What you need to know
The roads included in the new speed limit scheme would be B, C and unclassified routes within city confines.
Birmingham City Council has been considering the measure since it declared a road safety emergency in 2024, but plans would need to go through consultation. Mat MacDonald, road safety commissioner for the region, says he backs the idea.
Speaking to BBC Radio WM, MacDonald said the measure could stop tragedies such as the death of six-year-old Bobby Colleran, who was hit by a van in Liverpool in 2014.
“We know that if that van had been travelling at 20 rather than 30mph, which was the speed limit of that road… on a balance of probabilities he would still be alive today,” he said.
Would the new measure work?
The introduction of the same limit in Wales in 2024 saw around 100 fewer people being killed or seriously injured on relevant routes in its first year.
Birmingham City Council has recently reaffirmed its stance on the measures by putting them in its Local Plan – a document setting out how it can help influence the city’s future.
The student bank account perks – from takeaways to extra cash
Students soon to start their first year of university could snag themselves some extras and freebies by signing up to a student bank account.
With Lloyds, students can get a £100 sign-up bonus and up to £120 worth of Deliveroo vouchers if they meet certain conditions. Nationwide offers the same, but instead provide Just Eat vouchers.
If you open an account with Bank of Scotland and pay in at least £500 by 30 October, you’ll receive £100 in November. Then, you’ll get a £20 Deliveroo voucher for each month between November and April that you make 20 or more valid debit card transactions.
At NatWest, students get a welcome bonus of £100 and a four-year Tastecard for restaurant discounts. This card offers discounts on eating out, takeaways and entertainment.
What do other banks offer?
Santander students have access to a four-year railcard and cashback and reward schemes.
HSBC students get some discounts through their Home & Away scheme and access to a 5 per cent AER regular saver.
Starling offers a £50 Amazon gift card for students signing up and entry into a prize draw.
Barclays doesn’t offer extra perks, but offers an interest-free overdraft of up to £1,500.
Sterling charged with dangerous driving – what we know
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has been charged with dangerous driving and possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation after crashing into barriers on the M3 motorway.
No other vehicles were involved in the crash. The 31-year-old was also charged with failing to provide a specimen.
Sterling was arrested in May after he was filmed swerving his £270,000 Lamborghini and was released on bail. He is due to appear in court on 15 September.
Sterling’s career so far
Sterling enjoyed enormous success during his career in England, winning the Premier League four times with Manchester City and scoring 20 goals in 82 appearances for England.
His career took a sharp turn after he moved to Chelsea in 2022, after which he joined Dutch club Feyenoord last season. He is now without a club.
Meta agrees to pay up to $17bn to settle social media case
Meta has reached a settlement with US states and territories to resolve a court case related to child safety.
The agreement will require the social mediagiant to pay up to $17bn (£12.5bn).
What has Meta agreed to?
Meta agreed to establish safeguards for teenage users, including daily usage limits and night-time blocks nationwide in the US.
This is the first time Meta has been forced to change how its platforms function.
As part of the settlement, the company denies wrongdoing.
What happened at the trial?
It was alleged the company had violated numerous federal and state privacy laws for children.
The states suing Meta claimed it used its platforms “to ensnare youth and teens”, and ignored the damage they did to the “wellbeing of America’s youth”.
After the settlement was announced, District of Columbia attorney general Brian Schwalb called it a “monumental public health victory”.
What did Meta say?
Today, we are announcing an agreement with a bipartisan group of 52 attorneys general across US states, territories, and the District of Columbia, building on our long-standing efforts to empower parents and support teens
Calls for TikTok to follow
The company said TikTok and YouTube should also implement the same safety features for their younger users.
“Our new Time Limit commitments, Night Mode features and usage limits during school hours set the right path forward for our whole industry, but this framework will only work if all our peers join us,” Meta’s chief legal officer, CJ Mahoney, said.
These changes, which include daily time limits that can’t be turned off and muted notifications during school hours, will only be automatically applied to the accounts of those under 18 in “participating US states and territories”.
It means that young people in the UK will not be included in this raft of new safety measures. The Government said it is “following developments closely”.
Meta also pledged to continue to ensure only age-appropriate content is shown, stop unwanted contact from strangers, make it easy for teens to report concerning content and to block the ability for teens to add filters to their photos to make it look like they have had cosmetic surgery.
The technology giant says the new pledges are “building on our long-standing efforts to empower parents and support teens” and are billing the move as setting the “new industry standard”.
British children and teens using Facebook and Instagram currently have some protections in place already, with “Teen Accounts” which limits who can contact teens and places restrictions on the content they see.
The protections from Meta require a user to be honest about their age if they are a child, although protections are in place that require a user to submit ID or a video selfie if the system detects suspicious behaviour suggesting the user is lying about their age.
Children in the UK are also now protected by the Online Safety Act, which is being enforced by media regulator Ofcom.
It means that social media giants can be pursued if they are found to be putting children at risk online, including not taking adequate measures to prevent young people from viewing harmful content, including suicide and eating disorder posts.
The regulator launched an investigation into TikTok’s compliance with its child safety duties in July and said: “We’ve shown we’ll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short.”
Campaigners call for more action to protect children
Many campaigners say not enough is being done to protect children from online harms, with some calling for a complete ban on children under 16 using social media. Former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer announced that all British under-16s will be banned from major social media platforms, including TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat.
Online safety charity, the Molly Rose Foundation was set up by the father of Molly Russell, from Harrow in north-west London, who took her own life aged 14 in November 2017.
Rowan Ferguson, senior policy and public affairs manager at the organisation, said despite Molly dying nearly a decade ago due to the harms “Meta and other tech giants have repeatedly refused to tackle” – the settlement “demonstrates that big tech can and should be held to account”.
He added: “We have long been calling for action to address harmful and addictive design choices, underpinned by business models that prioritise profit over safety. This outcome demonstrates that, with the right motivation, change is possible.
“As these changes only apply to US users, the UK Government must heed this outcome and seize this opportunity to deliver a reset to children’s online safety across all platforms; Andy Burnham has now seen that it is possible to take on Big Tech to address drivers of online harm. It’s time for the UK Government to be brave, bold and decisive, in ways it hasn’t been before.”
Matt Navarra, an online safety expert, told The i Paper the restrictions on Meta’s titles in the US “gives the UK a very useful new benchmark” and the Government should “absolutely ask whether some of these protections should become minimum product standards here in the UK as well”.
He concluded: “You know, once a platform proves a safety feature is technically possible in one major market, it becomes much harder to explain why children elsewhere shouldn’t get those protections as well.”
Navarra said that paying out $18bn will not be “huge financial hit” for Meta, and “what matters more is that regulators are now reaching inside the product and dictating how Instagram and Facebook can engage teenagers“.
He explained: “For years, social media has basically been designed around, you know, keeping scrolling until you decide to stop and this starts flipping. that, you know, the big shift is from asking teenagers to protect themselves from pervasive kind of technology to requiring the technology to protect teenagers by default.”
Navarra also stressed that he does not believe “British children are suddenly less safe than American children” because “the UK already has the Online Safety Act and is moving towards tougher age restrictions”.
A Government spokespersonsaid: “While this is a matter for Meta and the US courts, we are following developments closely.”
They emphasised that the Online Safety Act requires platforms to protect users under 18 from harmful content and said: “We are already taking further steps to promote British children’s wellbeing and protect them from online harms by introducing a social media ban for under-16s next year.”
The spokesperson added: “We are also taking action on harmful features and addictive functionalities like limiting excess screen time and infinite scroll.”
An investigation by The i Paper in January 2025, after the Online Safety Act was brought in but before it was fully enforced, found that content which amplified feelings of depression and anger were repeatedly pushed to a social media profile set up for a 13-year-old boy even though he wasn’t searching for such content.
What safety changes has Meta promised for children in the US?
Meta has laid out 13 pledges that are set to be rolled out. It says they are “pending judicial approval” and will automatically apply to under-18s on Instagram and Facebook “in participating US states and territories”.
The technology giant states the “majority of the terms are required to remain in place for 10 years”.
Some features, including sleep time, study time and time limits, will not cover direct messages. Meta says this is to “allow teens to stay connected with friends and family”.
Time limits: A default daily time limit of two hours that can only be overridden by a parent, with that time covering use of both Facebook and Instagram. It will also encompass if a child has multiple accounts on those platforms.
Sleep time: Apps will be blocked between midnight and 6am.
Study time: Limits to the types of push notifications sent during school hours.
Nudges: Teens will be notified after 15 minutes of continuous screen time and once they have spent a total of 60 and 90 minutes on the apps.
No likes: The number of likes and reactions on posts will be hidden by default.
No filters: Child users will not be able to edit their photos to look like they have “extreme make-up” on.
Option for no autoplay: Teen accounts can opt to stop videos from starting automatically.
Option for no algorithms: There will be an option for feeds not to be personalised by the apps’ algorithms. This means the rolling suggested content on the app will not be determined by Meta’s technology, which is designed to show posts that have been calculated to be of interest to the user.
Age checks: Meta already says it actively tries to remove underage accounts from their apps, but has now pledged to invest “in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to under-13s”, as well as steps to identify accounts that may be between the ages of 13 and 17.
Boost for parents: New parental controls will be added to existing support, including notifying parents when a teen links a secondary account and alerting them to interactions with suspicious accounts.
Meta also pledged to continue to ensure only age-appropriate content is shown, stop unwanted contact from strangers, make it easy for teens to report concerning content and block the ability for teens to add filters to their photos to make it look like they have had cosmetic surgery.

sources.news_title: Tennessee to receive $750M of $17B Facebook, Instagram settlement
sources.text:
Tennessee will receive over $750 million as part of a nationwide $17.1 billion settlement by Meta Platforms, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram.
The company agreed to settle claims that it improperly collected data on minors and that its platforms are designed to addict children. In the settlement, Meta also agreed to impose daily time limits on children and prevent minors from using its platforms from midnight to 6 a.m., among several other provisions.
“We took Meta to trial because Instagram was hurting kids and misleading parents,” said Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti in a news release. “Now we’re ending the trial with a settlement that imposes unprecedented protections for kids.”
The money will go into a special fund managed by state officials called the Children’s Digital Protection Fund. The money can be used to fund research and treatment for children’s mental health and law enforcement-related activity to protecting minors.
The agreement comes as Meta’s trial with Tennessee in Nashville neared its end. Tennessee’s suit is part of a broader set of litigation by nearly every state, and this settlement also ends a separate federal trial against the company.
Meta is one of the largest publicly traded companies in the United States. It generated over $200 billion in revenue in 2025 and reported a net income of $60 billion.
C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a news release that the company was happy to reach an agreement with a bipartisan group of state attorneys general.
“The framework we’ve negotiated will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platforms,” Mahoney said. “Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away.”

sources.news_title: Meta will pay $18 billion for teen safety, asks TikTok and YouTube to follow suit
sources.text:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.
Meta will pay $18 billion for teen safety, asks TikTok and YouTube to follow suit
Aug 26, 2026 — 1:29 PM ET
- Meta has agreed to pay $18 billion as part of a settlement with 52 attorneys general over claims that Facebook and Instagram negatively impact teen mental health.
- The company has also implemented new default safeguards for teens that restrict access to core functions like Reels and Stories during certain times of the day.
- Around $5.3 billion of the overall $18 billion payout is conditioned on industry rivals TikTok and YouTube adopting similar measures.
For a while now, multiple studies have attempted to demonstrate how social media apps can have a detrimental impact on teen mental health. Meta-owned platforms like Instagram and Facebook have been at the center of discussions about the negative impact on children, and that’s led to some high-profile lawsuits. Today, Meta is ending one long legal battle by announcing a settlement with 52 attorneys general.
In a statement on its blog, Meta said it will pay around $18 billion as part of the settlement to fund youth online safety initiatives, along with other state activities. It further announced a long list of teen-safety features it will bundle into Facebook and Instagram, while also making some options the default for all teens. Notably, the company has denied any wrongdoing in this major settlement.
Among the measures adopted by Meta is a default 2-hour limit on Facebook and Instagram, with time spent scrolling across either app counting toward the combined limit. Meta mentions the “night mode” function, which disables the feed, Stories, and Reels between 12 AM and 6 AM. A similar mode is also in place for school time, which will mute Facebook and Instagram push notifications between 8 AM and 3 PM.
Crucially, the company notes that direct messaging will remain available during night mode, school mode, and the 2-hour limit “to stay connected with friends and family.” Furthermore, Meta says it will let teens turn off the algorithm-based feed and disable autoplay for content on these platforms.
Additionally, the company is blocking “extreme makeup filters,” while teens will also get prompts after 15 minutes of continuous screen time on either platform. The prompts will also appear after 60 and 90 minutes. Some of these options were already implemented by the two platforms over the past few years in response to growing concern over deteriorating teen mental health.
Are you happy with the steps taken by Meta to protect teen mental health?
On top of these measures, the social media giant is reportedly working on “stronger technology” to accurately detect accounts of under-13 users with falsified ages. It is also reportedly improving tech to better identify account owners between the ages of 13 and 17.
To make age detection easier, Meta urges app stores to provide verified age information so that social media platforms can tailor their experiences accordingly.
Meta agrees to shell out $18 billion, but with conditions
The company intends to pay out $12.7 billion to eligible states over the next decade in annual installments. However, the remaining $5.3 billion, or 30%, is tied to TikTok and Google-owned YouTube also adopting some of these measures.
These include implementing a one-hour daily limit on the use of those apps among teens, a nighttime cutoff, and measures to detect accounts of children with falsified age info. The second condition Meta imposed is that both TikTok and YouTube make a payment matching the 30% figure.
Additional input from Reuters reveals that $17.6 billion of the total amount will go to 48 US states, as well as Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands. Meanwhile, $459 million will be set aside for settling the Cambridge Analytica privacy claims from nearly a decade ago. The state of California will seemingly receive the largest payout at $2.2 billion, the report adds.
Some of the default behaviors implemented by Meta on both platforms will go a long way toward keeping teens away from its evidently addictive platforms. However, some of these problems cannot be truly solved until all platforms take these steps, just as Meta suggested. It will be interesting to see if TikTok and YouTube respond to the company’s call and put similar restrictions in place on their respective apps.

sources.news_title: END OF SOCIAL MEDIA? What Meta’s landmark case means for future of social media
sources.text:
Meta has agreed to a landmark settlement over allegations that its platforms harmed children and teenagers – raising a much bigger question about how social media is designed and regulated.
On this episode of The Fourcast, we look at what the settlement actually means for Instagram and Facebook users, whether other social media companies could be forced to follow suit, and whether this could fundamentally change the way we use social media.
Krishnan Guru-Murthy was joined by visiting professor at Stony Brook University School of Journalism and author of ‘Hot Type’ Jeff Jarvis and Associate Professor in Digital Humanities at University College London, Kaitlyn Regehr.
In a statement release after the settlement, Meta said the agreement is not an admission of wrongdoing, but a new framework designed to give parents more control and teenagers stronger protections. It says the measures will only work if TikTok and YouTube adopt the same rules, because teenagers move between multiple platforms.

sources.news_title: Maine to get $56M from Meta settlement over teen social media addiction
sources.text:
Meta agreed Wednesday to pay $17 billion in damages and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in a landmark legal settlement that ended a federal court battle over teen social media addiction and resolved claims filed by 47 states, including Maine.
Under the agreement, Maine will receive no less than $56 million, said state Attorney General Aaron Frey. The settlement is subject to court approval in the Northern District of California.
“This hard-fought settlement provides important protections for children on Meta’s platforms, Instagram and Facebook, and empowers parents with tools to help address the negative impacts of social media use on children,” Frey said via email.
Meta has agreed to measures designed to ensure that children age 12 and under cannot access its platforms and children ages 13-17 have limited access, Frey said.
The agreement — one of the largest state consumer protection settlements in history, after the $206 billion Big Tobacco settlement in 1998 — resolves a yearslong case aimed at holding the tech giant accountable for its role in grabbing children’s attention and harming their mental health.
“While this settlement is an important step, the need to make social media safer for children must extend to the entire industry,” Frey said. “We will continue to work with our multistate partners to push for comprehensive changes that prioritize the safety and welfare of children over profit.”
Gov. Janet Mills said the settlement will bring meaningful new protections, including bans on content that stokes mental health issues.
“For too long, social media has gone unregulated, harming the mental health of vulnerable children,” Mills said via email. “While there’s still much more to do to protect our kids online, I’m glad major corporations like Meta are finally being forced to make online spaces safer for our kids.”
Mills has long advocated for stronger online protections for Maine children. This year, she proposed and signed into law a statewide bell-to-bell cellphone ban in schools to end doomscrolling in classrooms, help students let go of addictive phones, and refocus school on education and community.
The states charged that Meta designed Instagram with addictive features, knowingly exposed young users to serious mental harms and intentionally misled the public about the safety of its platforms, among other things.
“This settlement is a victory for the protection of America’s children and an important first step to transform how the entire social media industry designs products for kids and teens,” Frey said.
Under the agreement, Meta must add daily time limits and “productive pauses” on most content to prevent teens from endless scrolling. Instagram and Facebook would have a combined two-hour daily time limit, with mandatory pauses after 15 minutes of continuous use and again at 60 and 90 minutes.
These limits are to remain in effect for five years. If Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube adopt comparable terms, the daily limit on each platform will drop to 60 minutes for 10 years.
Other safety features Meta must implement include nighttime blocks restricting teens access from midnight to 6 a.m.; push notification bans on school days from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m.; more effective age verification measures; and stronger safeguards against bullying.
Both the implementation and efficacy of the features will be regularly assessed by an independent auditor and the settling states, Frey said.
According to the settlement, which will be paid out over 10 years, the money can be used for a variety of purposes as deemed appropriate by each state’s attorney general, such as youth crisis intervention services, after-school or summer youth programs, public health advertising and youth mental health programs.
The attorneys general of Alabama, Alaska, American Samoa, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Northern Mariana Islands, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming joined the settlement.

sources.news_title: Nevada settles with Meta for $17.1 billion
sources.text:
Today, Attorney General Aaron D. Ford announced a landmark$17.1 billion multistate settlement with Meta Platforms, Inc. — one of the largest state consumer protection settlements in history outside the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s. In addition to the payment, Meta must implement a sweeping set of safety features designed to protect children on Instagram and Facebook. The agreement resolves claims by 47 states; Washington, D.C.; Puerto Rico; American Samoa; and the Northern Mariana Islands that the company designed Instagram with addictive features; knowingly exposed young users to serious mental harms; and intentionally misled the public about the safety of its platforms, among other things. This settlement is a monumental victory for the protection of America’s children and will fundamentally transform how the entire social media industry designs products for kids and teens. Under the settlement, the money that Nevada will receive could be as much as $255,930,000.00, with a guaranteed amount of $178,140,750.00 payable over 10 years.
“This settlement is a historic win for the safety and protection of our state’s youth and will hopefully be the first step toward a future in which social media companies do not treat our children as disposable products,” said Attorney General Ford. “This settlement will bring money into Nevada that will go directly toward educating and protecting our children, but, most importantly, it will implement changes that will drastically change how children can interact with Meta’s products. This settlement is strong, but it is not the end. I will continue to work to hold accountable the remaining social media companies who have unlawfully neglected to protect our children.”
The settlement requires Meta to implement a series of safety features on Instagram and Facebook, including:
- Hard cap daily time limits and “Productive Pauses” for children: for its two platforms, Instagram and Facebook, a combined two-hour daily time limit with mandatory pauses after 15 minutes of continuous use and again at 60 and 90 minutes to interrupt endless scrolling. These limits remain in effect for five years. If Snapchat, TikTok, and YouTube adopt comparable terms, the daily limit on each platform will drop to 60 minutes for 10 years.
- “Nighttime blocks” restricting children’s access from 12:00 a.m. to 6:00 a.m.
- Limited school-time access for children, eliminating push notifications on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. during the school year.
- Robust age assurance measures to more effectively verify the age of young users.
- Safer, age-appropriate content controls, including stronger safeguards against bullying; content promoting eating disorders; and content related to suicide and self-harm.
- Stronger, more user-friendly parental controls.
- Limits on social comparison features, including beauty filters and visible “like” counts, that have been linked to poor mental health outcomes in kids and teens.
- Both the implementation and efficacy of the features will be regularly assessed by an independent auditor and the settling states.
These are groundbreaking changes to Instagram and Facebook and more significant and comprehensive than previously ordered by any court. And perhaps most importantly, this settlement represents a down payment toward an industry-wide social media experience that allows kids to connect in a healthy way.
Attorney General Ford has made the defense of Nevada’s children from predatory social media companies a priority during his time in office. The Office of the Attorney General currently has lawsuits pending against TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Discord and Kik that accuse these companies of using harmful design features; failing to implement common-sense safety measures for children; and misleading the public regarding child users’ safety.
Several of the state’s lawsuits also include products liability claims and economic damages that are unique to the Nevada Attorney General’s jurisdiction to pursue consumer protection claims on behalf of Nevadans. In April, Attorney General Ford announced a first-of-its-kind agreement with the interactive game platform Roblox that will implement much-needed changes to protect Nevada’s children.
Beginning in 2021, nearly every attorney general in the country cooperated to investigate the social media industry for designing and promoting platforms to children and teens despite known harms. After a bipartisan, nationwide investigation found that Meta designed Instagram’s features to addict children while internally documenting the resulting mental health harms and failing to warn parents, many attorneys general sued Meta individually or as part of a consolidated federal lawsuit. This settlement resolves those cases and claims by the other settling states and territories. The settlement also resolves the states’ claims against Meta for its sharing of nonpublic information about Facebook users with third parties, like Cambridge Analytica, leading up to the 2016 election.
In addition to Attorney General Ford, the attorneys general of Alabama, Alaska, American Samoa, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Northern Mariana Islands, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming joined the settlement.

Meta to pay NH up to $224M as part of child safety trial settlement
sources.text:
New Hampshire will receive up to $224 million as part of agreement resolving lawsuits that claimed tech-giant Meta intentionally designed its products to addict young users and misrepresented the safety risks their social media platforms posed.
New Hampshire’s payout is part of a more than $17 billion multi-state deal, which includes 47 other states, Washington D.C. and numerous U.S. territories.
“Tech companies have used their algorithms and their platforms for profit to the detriment of a generation of children,” said Gov. Kelly Ayotte at a press conference in Concord Wednesday.
Research has shown that extensive screen use can lead to addiction-like behaviors and has been linked to issues like depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts in young people.
Ayotte called for further action to protect children online on both the state and federal level.
She said the state will use the money to bolster young people’s mental health and educate parents about tech platforms. But Ayotte and Attorney General John Formella said they did not yet know which specific initiatives will receive this funding.
Formella likened holding Meta accountable as akin to reining in big tobacco and opioid manufacturers.
“This case really began with a simple question: what responsibility does a company have when they design their products to addict kids? And when those products harm kids?” he said.
The settlement will also result in numerous product changes to protect Facebook and Instagram users under 18, including:
- a two-hour daily time limit on the platforms;
- restricted access overnight and during school hours;
- more stringent age verification measures; stricter limits on potentially harmful material such as things like eating disorders and self-harm;
- and more extensive parental controls. Formella said Meta will have to come into compliance within six months for the majority of changes, which will mostly be in place for 10 years.
The exact amount of money the state receives and the extent to which some of these product changes come into effect hinge on other social media giants, namely YouTube, TikTok and Snapchat, also agreeing to the terms of the settlement. Formella said 70% of the $224 million payout is guaranteed regardless, while the additional 30% depends on the other companies coming on board.
Formella said this settlement is the result of years-long coordination between nearly every attorney general in the country. He said more than 30 states joined a federal consolidated lawsuit filed in California, while New Hampshire filed its own lawsuit against Meta in state court, which was scheduled to go to trial in January 2027. This settlement ends New Hampshire’s case and other similar ones across the country.
Formella credited New Hampshire’s leadership in the lawsuit for the size of the payout it is slated to receive. He said typically states receive a recovery share roughly proportional to their population size, which in this case would be a guaranteed payout of $60 million. But, he said, the state is guaranteed to receive at least $158 million, nearly $100 million more than it usually would expect.
The money will be paid out in ten equal installments, the first coming roughly within the next month and the rest arriving annually on Jan. 15.

sources.news_title: Vermont to Receive $92.7 Million in Settlement With Meta
sources.text:
Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark on Wednesday announced that the state will receive a $92.7 million payout from tech giant Meta. The deal, which represents the largest single-company settlement in Vermont history, stems from a 2023 lawsuit alleging that the company knowingly put children in harm’s way through its “addictive” Instagram app and other social media platforms.
The state settlement is part of a larger one that will require Meta to pay at least $12.2 billion — and up to $17.1 billion — to 51 states and territories.
During a video press conference on Wednesday morning, Clark called the settlement “historic” and an example of what a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general can accomplish when they work together.
The settlement also requires Meta to make fundamental changes to Instagram and other Meta social media platforms for users under 18. The company must create an improved age-assurance process so that kids under 13 don’t use the platform and mandate a daily time limit of two hours a day. Meta has also agreed to ban the use of Instagram for children and teens between the hours of midnight to 6 a.m. and to ban notifications from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m. and during the school hours of 8 a.m. to 3 p.m.
The company has 15 to 30 days to make some of the changes, while others will take several months, according to Justin Kolber, chief of the Attorney General’s Office of Environmental and Public Protection Division.
The restrictions that Meta must put in place “will be incredibly helpful at getting us to a place where we can interface online and get the benefits but limit all of the risks that have been plaguing the mental health of young people, especially girls,” Clark said.
Vermont’s 114-page lawsuit against Meta alleged that Instagram violated the state’s Consumer Protection Act by “engaging in unfair and deceptive acts and practices in Commerce” by covering up the ways in which Instagram harms young people. The social media app causes them “to use the platform compulsively and excessively” through features such as infinite scroll and Reels, the suit said.
That causes myriad harm to youths, the suit asserted, including increased levels of anxiety and depression, sleep disruptions, and suicidal thoughts. It also exposes youths to harmful content, the suit said, including violence, adult sexual activity, and content that promotes extreme weight loss and disordered eating, which disproportionately harms teen girls.
Vermont may be eligible for an additional $34 million — bringing the total to $127 million — if other major social media companies, including TikTok, YouTube and Snap, enter into similar deals with the state, Clark said. In 2024, her office filed a still-pending lawsuit against TikTok related to its harm to youths.
The deal is what’s known as a “structured settlement,” meaning that Vermont will receive the money in annual installments of $8.8 million rather than a lump sum. The legislature will decide what to do with that money, Clark said, but her office is happy to advise the body on how it could be spent. Approximately $3.9 million of the payout to Vermont stems from a 2022 claim related to the company’s sale of personal data to third-party groups, including political analytics firm Cambridge Analytica, she said.
“We’ve seen a lot through the course of this investigation, and, frankly, our investigation of TikTok, that has inspired us to be advocates for change,” Clark said. “I think that passing that enthusiasm and knowledge on to the legislature is always helpful, but we are deferential to the legislature in fulfilling their role of spending the taxpayers’ money.”
Clark said on Wednesday that Vermont played a critical role in paving the way for the multistate settlement after the U.S. Supreme Court in May declined to hear an appeal by Meta in the state’s case. The company tried to get the lawsuit thrown out by asserting that it could not be sued in Vermont court because it had no specific ties here. The appeal followed a failed attempt by Meta in 2025 to have the case dismissed in the Vermont Supreme Court.
“This settlement is a watershed moment in the history of social media,” Clark said, one that will help usher in “an era where social media can be safer for children, safer for all of us.”
Correction, August 26, 2026: A previous version of this story misidentified Justin Kolber.

sources.news_title: Meta to Pay Tennessee Nearly $752 Million in Historic Settlement Over Instagram’s Alleged Harm to Kids
sources.text:
Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti announced Wednesday a landmark $17.1 billion multistate settlement with Meta Platforms, Inc., bringing an end to Tennessee’s lawsuit against the company over allegations that Instagram was designed to encourage addictive use among children and teens.
The settlement, described by Skrmetti’s office as the largest Big Tech settlement in history, requires Meta to pay $17.1 billion and implement sweeping new safety measures on Instagram and Facebook aimed at protecting young users.
🚨BIG WIN FOR TENNESSEE FAMILIES🚨
We took on one of the biggest tech companies in the world, and today, we’re holding Meta accountable.
Tennessee led 47 states and D.C., Puerto Rico, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands in a historic settlement over the impact of… pic.twitter.com/NDfn74IaT6
— TN Attorney General (@AGTennessee) August 26, 2026
Tennessee is set to receive almost $752 million from the agreement, which Skrmetti said will be directed to the state’s newly created Children’s Digital Protection Fund to support efforts to protect and restore the mental health and safety of Tennessee children.
“We took Meta to trial because Instagram was hurting kids and misleading parents,” Skrmetti said in a statement. “Now we’re ending the trial with a settlement that imposes unprecedented protections for kids and delivers record-setting money for Tennessee’s Children’s Digital Protection Fund.”
The settlement resolves claims brought by 47 states and several U.S. territories alleging Meta designed Instagram with addictive features, knowingly exposed young users to serious mental harms, and misled the public about the safety of its platforms.
The agreement comes just weeks after Tennessee began its trial against Meta in Davidson County Chancery Court. The lawsuit, filed by Skrmetti in October 2023, alleged that Meta deliberately engineered Instagram to maximize engagement among young users while concealing risks associated with the platform.
Skrmetti previously identified the lawsuit as a top priority and told The Tennessee Star’s CEO and Editor-in-Chief Michael Patrick Leahy in April that his office had assembled a specialized trial team to take on Meta.
“They have optimized their product over decades using neuroscientists and casino designers and A/B testing on the big scale level,” Skrmetti said at the time, arguing that Meta could make its products safer for children.
Under the settlement unveiled on Wednesday, Instagram and Facebook will impose a combined daily limit of two hours for young users, with mandatory pauses after 15 minutes of continuous use and again at 60 and 90 minutes. The limits will remain in place for five years.
The platforms will also restrict young users’ access between midnight and 6 a.m., eliminate weekday push notifications from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. during the school year, strengthen age verification and parental controls, and impose additional safeguards involving bullying, eating disorders, suicide, and self-harm content.
The agreement will also limit certain social-comparison features for young users, including beauty filters and visible “like” counts.
“This is a generational win for our state and for our kids,” Skrmetti said.
The settlement follows a nationwide investigation that began in 2021 involving attorneys general from across the country. Skrmetti said Tennessee’s case, along with related federal litigation, helped spur negotiations that ultimately produced the agreement.
Skrmetti also said the settlement should serve as a first step toward broader federal regulation of technology companies that interact with children, while calling for Congress to establish a federal duty of care for platforms serving young users.
“This settlement is the best possible solution we could get through litigation, and it delivers serious accountability with both comprehensive injunctive terms and record-setting money. But in the long run, we need federal legislation that clearly imposes a duty of care on every tech company that interacts with kids,” he said.
While Meta welcomed the agreement as a new standard for teen safety, it called on TikTok and YouTube to adopt the same protections, arguing that teens move between multiple platforms.
“Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away,” Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said.
– – –
Kaitlin Housler is a reporter at The Tennessee Star and The Star News Network.

sources.news_title: Missouri to receive at least $100 million in Meta settlement
sources.text:
Missouri to receive at least $100 million in Meta settlement
COLUMBIA, Mo. (KMIZ)
The State of Missouri is set to receive millions of dollars as part of a $17.1 billion settlement with Meta Platforms, Inc.
According to a news release from Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, Missouri will receive between $100 million and $150 million.
“As a mother, I know how critical it is to shield kids from predators, addictive material, and content that harms their mental health," Hanaway said in a statement.
According to the settlement, payments will be made within 30 days after a state enters a consent judgment or formally agrees to the settlement.
It is unclear if Missouri has filed for a consent judgment.
Once received, it will be up to the General Assembly to distribute funds. The final consent judgment from Tennessee's suit suggests funds go to public programs like crisis intervention services, after-school and summer programs or internet safety training.
Along with resolving claims in 47 states, the settlement also requires Meta to add new safety features for child and teen Instagram and Facebook accounts. The new safety features will be in place until 10 years after the settlement takes effect.
These features include:
- Mandatory "Productive Pauses" to break up lengths of endless social media use. There will be a warning at 15 minutes, a break at 60 minutes then another break at 90 minutes.
- "Nighttime blocks" to restrict access to only messages from midnight to 6 a.m.
- Limiting push notifications on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. during the school year.
- Extensive age verification measures
- Stronger parental and content controls, limiting content that may promote eating disorders or self-harm
- Limits on features like beauty filters and "like" counts
Meta will also work to promote parental controls over underage accounts. If linked to an account, parents would be able to see how long their child spends on social media, usernames of their child's social media connections as well as profiles of reported accounts. Parents will also be notified if their child repeatedly searches for terms related to suicide, self-harm or eating disorders.
Hickman High School 11th-grade students, Ava McKinney and Adrienne Martin, are not opposed to the changes.
"I immediately get on social media when I go home, it's just what I do," McKinney said. "I think the limits are really good because spending more than 5 hours on social media is like not good, you could be spending that time doing homework, socializing, doing stuff with your family."
"Four or five hours, once I get home on Social media, I mean, I know it's not healthy, but it's just addictive," Martin said. "The limit for beauty filters is awesome because again, insecurity is a really big thing, especially with like young teenage girls, beauty filters are not something that should be normalized."
"Meta’s willingness to acknowledge the harm and take meaningful corrective action is an important step forward for the safety of children across the country," Hanaway said in a statement.
The lawsuit began in 2021 when states began to investigate the social media industry, claiming major companies knew of the harm social media causes. Meta did not admit wrongdoing as part of the settlement.

sources.news_title: CT Could Receive $265M In Settlement With Facebook Parent Company
sources.text:
HARTFORD, CT — A landmark $17.1 billion settlement with Meta Platforms, Inc. will enforce sweeping new safety reforms on Instagram and Facebook, according to Attorney General William Tong.
The agreement between Meta and 51 attorneys general will see Connecticut receive up to $265.4 million, with at least half of all funds directed to remediate youth harms from social media, including but not limited to support for mental health and crisis intervention, after school and summer school programming, and implementation of phone-free school zones.
The agreement resolves claims that the company designed Instagram with addictive features, knowingly exposed young users to serious mental harms, and intentionally misled the public about the safety of its platforms, among other things. The settlement also resolves the multistate investigation led by Connecticut against Meta for its sharing of nonpublic information about Facebook users with third parties, like Cambridge Analytica, leading up to the 2016 election.
“Meta strip-mined the souls of America’s children for maximum profit with abusive and addictive features that unleashed a youth mental health catastrophe. That ends now,” Tong said in a Wednesday morning press conference. “This settlement charts a new course for online safety, enforcing sweeping reforms to fundamentally alter the experience for kids on Instagram and Facebook.”
Tong said Meta must deploy robust age verification measures, online time caps, parental options to turn off algorithmic feeds and auto-play functions and content moderation, among other measures.
“We will aggressively monitor this rollout and will not hesitate to return to court to protect the safety of our kids online,” Tong said. “To TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat — our expectations are clear. You’re next.”
Meta, in a statement posted to its website, said the agreement built on its longstanding efforts to empower parents and teens.
“Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta,” the statement read. “We want to get this right for parents and teens, and that’s why we partnered with state attorneys general to set a new industry standard.”
The company also called on TikTok and Youtube to join the agreement.
“All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place, because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another,” the company said.
Under the terms of the agreement, Meta must pay states $12.19 billion over 10 years. That amount increases to $17.1 billion contingent on TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat, each facing state enforcement actions and investigations, agreeing to comparable safety terms and monetary relief. The settlement is subject to the approval of United States District Court Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers of the Northern District of California.
Gov. Ned Lamont said the agreement was long overdue.
“Social media is all too often anti-social,” he said. “Tech companies have increasingly been taking advantage of kids, creating apps and algorithms that decrease their attention spans, drive them to become addicted, cause them to tune out real life, and harmfully impact their mental health and wellbeing.”
North Haven state Sen. Paul Cicarella, the ranking Republican on the General Law Committee, said the legislature would remain vigilant in protecting young people.
“As state lawmakers, we have been consistently and effectively working to combat the ill-effects of social media on children,” he said. “This historic settlement will hold these providers accountable.”
Kate Dias, president of the Connecticut Education Association, said the settlement demonstrated that children were defenseless against multibillion-dollar corporations.
“We have an obligation to protect our children, to build spaces where they can become vibrant, where they can live beautiful, robust lives, where maybe they can make mistakes without fear of them becoming part of their digital footprint for the rest of their lives,” she said.

sources.news_title: Alabama to receive $117 million from Meta lawsuit
sources.text:
MONTGOMERY, Ala. — Alabama will soon receive more than $117 million as part of a multistate settlement with Meta Platforms Inc., owner of Facebook, over allegations tied to the safety of kids using Instagram and Facebook, according to a press release made Wednesday by Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall.
The agreement resolves claims brought by 47 states, claiming Meta designed Instagram to be addictive, as well as exposing young people to mental health risks, and misleading the public about the platform’s safety.
“This settlement sends a clear message that Alabama will hold big tech accountable when it fails to protect our children online,” Marshall said.
The agreement will also require Meta to put in place a series of safety measures for young people.
One change includes a two-hour daily limit for children using either Instagram or Facebook alongside mandatory breaks after 15 minutes of nonstop use and again at 60 and 90 minutes. Those limits are set to remain in place for five years.
Children will also have nighttime restrictions from midnight to 6 a.m. Push notifications will be disabled on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. during the school year.
Other provisions require more rigorous age-verification, extra parental controls, tighter restrictions on content involving bullying, eating disorders, suicide, and self-harm.
Marshall said his office will continue monitoring Meta’s compliance with the settlement.
The agreement follows other actions by Marshall’s office involving technology companies, including a settlement with Roblox and an ongoing lawsuit against TikTok that is scheduled for trial in September.

sources.news_title: Meta reaches $17 billion settlement with states over landmark teen social media addiction claims
Massachusetts to receive up to $516M in Meta settlement, Campbell says
sources.text:
BOSTON — Attorney General Andrea Campbell announced Wednesday that she and a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general reached a $17.1 billion settlement with Meta — including a guarantee of approximately $366 million for Massachusetts.
The settlement, which Campbell's office said is the largest state consumer protection win in history outside the "Big Tobacco" settlements in the 1990s, is subject to court approval. Those funds would resolve claims of Facebook's failure to protect consumers' private information from mishandling by Cambridge Analytica and Facebook's alleged continued misrepresentation to users.
If approved, Massachusetts could get up to $516 million from Meta, including a guaranteed $366 million over the next decade.
"As a mom and as Attorney General, I know that young people deserve to grow up in a world where they can benefit from technology without being exploited by it. We took on Meta because the company chose to put profits ahead of the wellbeing of young people," Campbell said in a press release. "This settlement is about more than a financial penalty — it's about changing the way Big Tech does business. We secured meaningful, long-term changes to Meta's products and practices, while delivering real resources to Massachusetts."
Campbell's office said the funding would go toward rectifying harms young people in Massachusetts have faced as a result of social media, including: efforts to expand youth crisis intervention and mental health services; helping after-school, summer and outdoor programs; boosting digital wellness and literacy; supporting phone-free school efforts; and training medical providers on social media use and body dysmorphia. Some of the funds would also go to the state General Fund.
The settlement would also bar users under 13 from using Instagram or Facebook and those aged 13 to 18 would have certain account protections added over the next four to six months.
These protections include a daily time limit of 120 minutes across Instagram and Facebook, blocking teen user access between midnight and 6 a.m. as well as barring notifications between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m., and silenced notifications during typical school hours of 8 a.m. to 3 p.m.
Under the settlement, Meta would also be required to implement an "enhanced age assurance framework" to identify users under 13 and those between the ages of 13 and 18 "with a high level of accuracy," according to Campbell's office. That framework wouldn't require users to submit government identification or "other sensitive information" for age verification.
Teens would also notice several changes to the platforms including prompts that show options to turn off "autoplay" and personalized algorithmic feed features. Campbell's office said there will be "prominent" pauses and breaks after 15 minutes of continuous use along with breaks at 60 minutes and 90 minutes of cumulative use. Teens can disable like counts and other counts of social reactions and disable filters that imitate cosmetic surgery.
Also, teens' accounts on Meta platforms would be defaulted to private and adults who a "teen does not affirmatively connect to" would be restricted from messaging them or seeing their accounts, according to Campbell's office. Parents could enable protective settings and get information on their teens' time spent on platforms, content searches and contact with adult users.
The settlement would bring the state's years-long litigation against Meta to a close. In 2023, Campbell sued Meta alleging Meta violated state law "by purposefully designing their applications to addict young users, and actively and repeatedly deceiving the public about the danger posed to young people by overuse of their products."
Attorneys for Meta did not immediately respond to the News Service's request for comment on the settlement.
The settlement comes as Beacon Hill negotiators are hashing out the details of legislation (H 5366 / S 3175) regulating social media access for kids and teens.
The House's bill bans kids under 14 from using social media platforms and requires parental consent for users aged 14 and 15. The legislation also requires platforms to prohibit users aged 14 or 15 from accessing addictive social feeds and users of those ages could not receive social media notifications between midnight and 6 a.m.
As far as age verification, the bill calls on social media platforms to "implement an age assurance or verification system to determine whether a current or prospective user on the social media platform meets the age requirement."
The Senate's legislation skipped the social media ban the House adopted, but also requires social media platforms to adopt "default" settings for minors that disable features like addictive feeds and autoplay. Also, the legislation bans notifications to minors between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. and requires platforms to offer at least one age verification method that doesn't require users to submit biometric data or a government ID.

NJ to receive $565M+ from Facebook owner over teen addiction claims
sources.text:
NJ to receive $565M+ from Facebook owner over teen addiction claims
Agreement requires platforms adopt many of the limits signed into NJ law earlier in August
Facebook owner Meta agreed to pay nearly $18 billion to an array of U.S. states over claims its platforms intentionally addicted teens. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Facebook’s owner agreed to pay New Jersey more than $565 million as part of a landmark settlement resolving claims by 47 states, the District of Columbia, and some U.S. territories who charged the tech giant violated child privacy and intentionally built addictive features that exposed young users to mental harms.
As part of the settlement agreement, which does not carry an admission of guilt and must still be approved by the courts, tech giant Meta agreed to institute new limits like daily caps on underage users’ social media activity, subject its platforms to independent auditing, and limit the discoverability of teens’ accounts, among other things.
“As a parent, protecting your kids is always your North Star, and this agreement achieves critical protections for our children today,” New Jersey Attorney General Jen Davenport said in a statement Wednesday.
Meta agreed to pay the states and others who sued a combined $17.1 billion. New Jersey, which was among the first states to sue Meta, will receive between $525 million and $752 from a portion of the settlement covering the firm’s use of addictive features and its minimization of their harms.
New Jersey will also receive $20.3 million over privacy claims related to Cambridge Analytica, the now-defunct firm that improperly acquired access to the private data of millions of Facebook users while aiding President Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.
In total, Meta agreed to pay $459.3 million to plaintiffs to resolve claims stemming from Cambridge Analytica, plus $75 million for litigation costs.
The settlement agreement requires Facebook to erect an array of new limits on teens’ social media use.
Those include provisions to block teens’ access to social media platforms between midnight and 6 a.m. and others to limit push notifications from the platforms between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m.
The settlement also requires the tech firm limit teens’ access to its platforms during school hours and regularly present teen users with the option to switch to a non-personalized feed.
The agreement requires Meta to cap teens’ daily use to two hours across all its platforms, which include Facebook, Instagram, and Threads, with periodic notifications to pause after 60 and 90 minutes of cumulative use in a given day.
“Today’s settlement is a major victory for New Jersey families. Big Tech is finally being held accountable for the harm it is causing, especially to our children’s mental health and safety. More important, parents and teens will finally get some relief, including groundbreaking new safety features to protect kids online,” said Gov. Mikie Sherrill. “But here in New Jersey, we won’t stop fighting until all of the Big Tech companies follow suit.”
Many of the settlement’s restrictions mirror New Jersey statute that Sherrill signed into law earlier this month.
In an unsigned statement, Meta said teens’ safety is paramount for its platforms but warned the changes may be less impactful if younger users migrate to other social media platforms not subject to the settlement’s provisions.
“We know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another,” it said in the statement. “For meaningful progress to happen, we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard, to ensure teens use social media in a healthy and responsible way.”
Other parts of the settlement require Meta to block teens from seeing like counts, limit unrelated adults’ ability to find their accounts, and step up its own age verification efforts.

sources.news_title: Nebraska to receive up to $201 million from Meta landmark settlement
sources.text:
LINCOLN — Nebraska will receive up to $201 million from the Meta landmark settlement, Attorney General Mike Hilgers said Wednesday morning.
Nebraska’s sum is part of a larger settlement of $17.1 billion with 47 states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories over claims that the company knowingly designed and deployed harmful features on its social media platforms intended to addict children and teens. As part of the settlement, Meta has agreed to implement changes to its platforms for younger users.
Hilger called Wednesday’s announcement of the settlement “one of the biggest days” in the history of the Nebraska AG office.
“We have achieved some of the most important relief … both for the state to help abate the impact of social media on kids, but also to empower parents to help protect kids,” he said during his press conference.
The settlement ends the trial of the case that began in California last week, which had been expected to last six to eight weeks.
The changes for younger users of Facebook and Instagram will include hard-cap daily time limits and “productive pauses” — a combined two-hour daily time limit with mandatory pauses after 15 minutes of continuous use and again at 60 and 90 minutes to interrupt endless scrolling.
Other changes include:
- “Nighttime blocks” restricting children’s access from midnight to 6 a.m.
- Limited school-time access and no push notifications for children on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. during the school year.
- Robust age assurance measures to more effectively verify the age of young users.
- Safer, age-appropriate content controls, including stronger safeguards against bullying, content promoting eating disorders, and content related to suicide and self-harm.
- Stronger, more user-friendly parental controls.
Most of these changes will be effective for a decade.
Hilgers said the funds will go to the state’s consumer protection cash fund; he added that it will be up to the Legislature and the governor how the money will be used. Meta, in a statement, said the fund “can be used to fund youth online safety initiatives, among other state priorities.”
Nebraska will also get $5.1 million from Meta for its “sharing of nonpublic information about Facebook users with third parties, like Cambridge Analytica, leading up to the 2016 election.”
Cambridge Analytica, which had ties to former Trump political strategist Steve Bannon, purchased Facebook data on tens of millions of Americans without their knowledge to target U.S. voters during the 2016 Trump campaign, according to AP.
In the same statement, Meta called on YouTube and TikTok to implement similar changes on their platforms.
“For meaningful progress to happen, we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard, to ensure teens use social media in a healthy and responsible way,” part of the statement reads.

sources.news_title: Meta joins a list of corporations that have settled cases for billions of dollars
sources.text:
Meta joins a list of corporations that have settled cases for billions of dollars
Tech giant Meta has agreed to pay $17 billion as part of a settlement to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction, state attorneys general announced Wednesday
Tech giant Meta has agreed to pay $17 billion as part of a settlement to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction, state attorneys general announced Wednesday. While the settlement is a fraction of Meta’s 2025 revenue of $201 billion, it’s still among one of the biggest corporate settlements ever. Here’s a look at some other large corporate settlements.
Tech giant Meta this week agreed to pay $17 billion as part of a settlement to end a landmark trial related to safeguards for younger users of social media. It is one of the largest such settlements ever, though it represents only a fraction of the $201 billion in revenue that the company booked last year.
Here's a look at some other notable corporate settlements.
BP and the Deepwater Horizon disaster
Oil giant BP agreed to pay $20 billion for the Deepwater Horizon disaster that became the worst offshore spill in the nation’s history.
The settlement, first announced in 2016, included $5.5 billion in civil Clean Water Act penalties and billions more to cover environmental damage and other claims by the five Gulf states and local governments. The money is to be paid out over roughly 16 years.
Enron and its massive accounting scandal
Enron, once the nation’s seventh-largest company, filed for bankruptcy protection in 2001, after years of accounting tricks could no longer hide billions of dollars in debt or make failing ventures appear profitable. The energy company’s collapse put more than 5,000 people out of work and wiped out more than $2 billion in employee pensions.
Twenty-four Enron executives, including former CEO Jeffrey Skilling, were convicted for their roles in the fraud.
A class-action lawsuit led to the recovery of more than $7 billion in funds.
WorldCom hid falling profits in one of the worst cases of accounting fraud
WorldCom Inc. collapsed and went into bankruptcy in 2002 following revelations of an $11 billion accounting fraud that included pressure from top executives on subordinates to inflate numbers to make the company seem more profitable. The collapse caused losses to stockholders, including those who had invested through retirement plans.
In 2005, the company agreed to pay shareholders about $750 million in cash and stock, while major banks and accounting firms settled for about $6 billion.
WorldCom's former CEO, Bernie Ebbers was convicted in New York in 2005 on securities fraud and other charges and received a 25-year sentence. He died in 2020, just over a month after his early release from prison.
After its collapse, WorldCom reemerged under a new name, MCI. It was taken over by Verizon and relocated its operations to Ashburn, Virginia.
JPMorgan, Bank of America and the housing bets that shook the world
JPMorgan Chase & Co. agreed to pay $13 billion in a landmark settlement in 2013. The firm acknowledged that it misled investors about the quality of risky mortgage-backed securities ahead of the 2008 financial crisis.
The agreement also included settlements with New York, California and other states.
JPMorgan was among the major banks that sold securities that plunged in value when the housing market collapsed in 2006 and 2007. Those losses triggered a financial crisis that pushed the economy into the worst recession since the 1930s.
A year later, Bank of America reached a $16.65 billion settlement with the government over the same issue. Its deal called for the bank, the second-largest in the U.S., to pay a $5 billion cash penalty, another $4.6 billion in remediation payments and provide about $7 billion in relief to struggling homeowners.
Johnson & Johnson and the marathon legal fight over talc
Johnson & Johnson agreed in July to pay $5.5 billion after fighting lawsuits for almost two decades over talc products that plaintiffs claimed had caused ovarian cancer.
The drugmaker, which has been fighting talc-related lawsuits for more than a decade, said that the settlement is conditioned on at least 95% of remaining claimants participating.
A U.S. bankruptcy court judge denied a $9 billion settlement proposed by company subsidiary Red River Talc last year that would have been one of the biggest mass tort settlements in history.
Johnson & Johnson decided not to appeal that ruling and instead fight on in court.
As part of the proposed settlement, Johnson & Johnson will make an initial payment of no more than $3 billion next year. It has no additional payments due until 2028.
